# Worksheet: events that change an epidemic

**~45 minutes**

The session showed you a **lockdown**: a callback that changes a *parameter* at
scheduled times. Here you will build the other two members of the same family:
a **vaccination pulse**, which changes the *state*, and a **capacity-triggered
lockdown**, which fires when the epidemic itself crosses a threshold rather than
at a time you picked in advance.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating, so ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there;
not reaching it is completely fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of
each day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

**Prefer sliders to typing?** The
[Pluto notebook](../../notebooks/chapters/03-ordinary-differential-equations.jl)
for this chapter lets you drag the lockdown parameters and watch the curve
respond. Some people find it easier to get the intuition there first and then
come back here. Either order is fine.

**Coming from R?**

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `f <- function(x) x^2` | `f(x) = x^2` | or `function f(x) ... end` |
| `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` | `x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` | `1.0` and `1` are different types |
| `sapply(v, f)` | `f.(v)` | the dot applies `f` elementwise |

Indexing starts at 1, as in R. A `!` at the end of a name (`sir_ode!`) means the
function modifies its argument rather than returning a copy.

The [Julia essentials chapter](../../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd)
has the full table.

## Setup

This is the model from the session, given so you can get straight to the new
material. Run it and check the output looks familiar.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-setup
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using DiffEqCallbacks
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end

u0    = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p     = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
tspan = (0.0, 80.0)
tt    = 0.0:0.25:80.0

sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(sol[2, :]), digits = 1))
println("final size (R at day 80): ", round(sol(80.0)[3], digits = 1))
```

---

## Part A — a vaccination pulse (~15 min)

The lockdown in the session changed a **parameter**:
`integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = β_lock,))`.

A vaccination campaign is different. It does not change how transmission works.
It moves people. On the day of the campaign, some fraction of the susceptibles
becomes immune immediately. That is a change to the **state**,
`integrator.u`, not to the parameters.

Susceptibles who are vaccinated move straight to $R$:

$$
S \rightarrow S - fS, \qquad R \rightarrow R + fS
$$

for a coverage fraction $f$, applied once on day $t_v$.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-a1
t_vax = 10.0     # day of the campaign
f_vax = 0.30     # fraction of susceptibles reached
vaccinated = Float64[]     # record of how many the campaign reached

function vaccinate!(integrator)
    moved = 0.0        # TODO: replace 0.0 — how many people does the campaign reach?
    # TODO: remove them from S (integrator.u[1])
    # TODO: add them to R (integrator.u[3])
    push!(vaccinated, moved)
end

vax_cb  = PresetTimeCallback([t_vax], vaccinate!)
sol_vax = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
                callback = vax_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

# R now holds recovered and vaccinated people alike, so the number ever infected
# is no longer just R(80) — subtract the people the campaign put there.
ever_infected = sol_vax(80.0)[3] - sum(vaccinated)
baseline_infected = sol(80.0)[3]
peak_vax = maximum(sol_vax(t)[2] for t in tt)
peak_base = maximum(sol(t)[2] for t in tt)

check("population still conserved",
      all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), sol_vax.u))
check("the campaign moved people out of S", sum(vaccinated) > 1.0)
check("the peak is lower", peak_vax < 0.8 * peak_base)
check("fewer people were ever infected", ever_infected < baseline_infected - 50)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
moved = f_vax * integrator.u[1]
integrator.u[1] -= moved
integrator.u[3] += moved
```

If the conservation check fails, you have probably added people to $R$ without
taking them out of $S$. A campaign moves people, it does not create them.
:::

### A1. Interpret

After the campaign, $R$ holds vaccinated people as well as recovered ones, which
is why the code above subtracts `sum(vaccinated)` before reporting how many were
ever infected.

- What would you have concluded about the campaign if you had reported $R(80)$
  directly instead?
- `moved` is a number of people, not a rate. How does that show up in the shape
  of the curve at day 10?

> *Your answer here.*

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch03-vax
#| fig-cap: "Infectious curve with and without a vaccination pulse on day 10."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)")
vlines!(ax, [t_vax]; color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "campaign")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "no vaccination")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_vax(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "vaccination on day $(Int(t_vax))")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

## Part B — when should the campaign happen? (~15 min)

The loop below runs the campaign on three different days and reports the final
size, the total number of people ever infected.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-b1
function ever_infected_with_vaccination(day)
    moved_by_campaign = Float64[]
    # `affect!` is defined inside this function so that it can see
    # `moved_by_campaign` — each call gets a fresh, separate record.
    affect!(integrator) = begin
        moved = f_vax * integrator.u[1]
        integrator.u[1] -= moved
        integrator.u[3] += moved
        push!(moved_by_campaign, moved)
    end
    s = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
              callback = PresetTimeCallback([day], affect!),
              reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
    return s(80.0)[3] - sum(moved_by_campaign)
end

campaign_days = Float64[]   # TODO: fill this list — try days 5, 20, and 40

for d in campaign_days
    println("campaign on day $d → $(round(ever_infected_with_vaccination(d), digits = 1)) ever infected")
end

check("three days tried", length(campaign_days) == 3)
```

### B1. Interpret

- Which campaign day gives the smallest final size?
- The same 30% coverage produces very different results depending on timing. Why?
  Think about how many susceptibles are left to protect on each of those days.

> *Your answer here.*

::: {.callout-note}
We are comparing three timings we chose by hand. The interventions and
optimization session is where an optimizer searches the timings for you. Today is
about expressing the event; choosing between events comes later.
:::

## Part C — a lockdown that triggers itself (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

The session's lockdown and your vaccination pulse both happened on a day fixed in
advance. Real policy often responds to the epidemic instead: *impose restrictions
when hospital occupancy crosses a threshold*.

That needs a `ContinuousCallback`, which watches a quantity you define and fires
the moment it crosses zero. The session used one to find the epidemic peak by
watching $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$. Here you watch the gap between infectious
numbers and a capacity limit:

$$
\text{condition} = I(t) - \text{capacity}.
$$

When that hits zero, transmission drops, and unlike the scheduled lockdown we did
not have to know in advance when it would happen. In code the condition is handed
three arguments, `(u, t, integrator)`; here only `u` is needed.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-c1
capacity = 100.0
trigger_day = Float64[]

# TODO: replace 0.0 — the gap between infectious numbers and capacity
capacity_condition(u, t, integrator) = 0.0

function impose_restrictions!(integrator)
    integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = 0.02,))     # β drops
    push!(trigger_day, integrator.t)
end

cap_cb  = ContinuousCallback(capacity_condition, impose_restrictions!)
sol_cap = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
                callback = cap_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

check("the trigger fired", !isempty(trigger_day))
check("restrictions kept I near capacity",
      maximum(sol_cap(t)[2] for t in tt) < 1.1 * capacity)

isempty(trigger_day) || println("restrictions imposed on day ",
                                round(trigger_day[1], digits = 2))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

The condition is just `u[2] - capacity`. `ContinuousCallback` root-finds it, so
you get the crossing time to solver accuracy rather than to the nearest saved
point.

Watch the two spellings of the state. A *condition* is handed the state directly,
so it uses `u[2]`. An *affect!* is handed the whole integrator and reaches inside
it, so Part A wrote `integrator.u[1]`. Writing `integrator.u[2]` here would work
too, but `u` is already right there.
:::

### C1. Interpret

Compare this with Part A. Both reduce the epidemic, but one required you to name
a date and the other did not.

- What does the triggered version need you to know in advance that the scheduled
  version does not, and vice versa?
- The restrictions here never lift. What would you need to add for them to?

> *Your answer here.*
